736.title: Yudhishthira stays put
736.hook: the brothers know the house will burn, and the son of Dharma weighs it: why Hindus call dharma subtle
736.carry: dharma is subtle, not a rulebook
736.tomorrow: who sleeps in the house the night it burns?
736.howItsDone: Hindu teachers still quote the Mahabharata's line that dharma is subtle when a hard choice has no easy rule; Yudhishthira, called Dharmaraja, is the epic's picture of a man who has to weigh it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vidura's riddle, and Yudhishthira catching the smell of fat and lac. Your line: dharma protects those who protect it.

Bhima's answer is the obvious one. If this house is made to burn, let's get out of it, back to where we were safe. It's the answer that comes first, standing in a room that smells of fuel. The walls look solid. The rooms are fine. Purochana is all smiles. And somewhere in the plaster is enough to turn the whole place into a torch. Yudhishthira says no. We stay.
screen: `BHIMA: LET'S GET OUT.` → `THE WALLS LOOK SOLID.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA: WE STAY.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira lays out his reasons. If we run, Purochana will know we've guessed, and he'll set the fire at once, or Duryodhana's people will hunt us down. We have no allies out here, no treasury, no army. So we'll live here as if we suspect nothing. We'll go hunting, learn every road and path, and make a way out nobody can see. Then help arrives: a skilled digger, sent by Vidura, who proves himself by repeating words from the riddle on the road. From the middle of the house he digs a passage out, and covers its mouth level with the floor. Purochana keeps watch at the door, sure his guests know nothing. Now look at who made that call. Yudhishthira is the son of Dharma, the god of right order, and the most truthful of the brothers. You'd expect the rule-keeper to do the simple thing: accuse the liar, or walk out. Instead he weighs it, and chooses to keep quiet, to keep his mother and brothers alive. The Mahabharata has a phrase for moments like this, and it comes back again and again: dharma is subtle. Dharma is one of Hinduism's biggest words: the right way, the duty that holds a life and a world together. And for Hindus it isn't a rulebook you look up. It's a weighing: who is at risk, what's true, what each choice sets off. Even the son of Dharma has to think. So the brothers eat in the house, sleep in the house, smile at Purochana, and wait, the text says, a long time, with weapons close at hand.
screen: `IF WE RUN, HE BURNS IT NOW.` · `VIDURA'S DIGGER, AND A HIDDEN PASSAGE.` · `THE SON OF DHARMA WEIGHS IT.` · then, large: `DHARMA IS SUBTLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one choice in front of you that isn't simple, where two good things pull different ways. If you pray, say Om softly three times first. If you don't, just breathe. Then don't decide yet. Weigh it the way Yudhishthira did: who could be hurt, what's true, what each choice would set off. Let the body be calm while the mind stays awake.
The lac house. The brothers stay, calm on the surface, while Vidura's digger cuts a hidden passage under the floor.
Your line: dharma is subtle, not a rulebook. Even the son of Dharma had to weigh it. Tomorrow, the night comes. See you then.

737.title: The ones with no names
737.hook: strangers sleep in the house the night it burns, and why Hindus say one Self lives in every being
737.carry: the wise see one self in every being
737.tomorrow: who is waiting at the river?
737.howItsDone: In Pitru Paksha, the fortnight for the ancestors, many Hindus offer water and sesame, tarpana, for the dead; some tarpana prayers include those who have no relatives to remember them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yudhishthira chose to stay, calm on the surface, while Vidura's digger cut a passage under the floor. Your line: dharma is subtle, not a rulebook.

The house at Varanavata was made to look like a gift and burn like a torch, with lac, resin and ghee worked into its walls, the text says. Under its floor is a different secret: a tunnel, dug by a miner Vidura sent, its mouth hidden inside the house. Kunti and her sons are living on top of a fire that hasn't been lit. Purochana, who built it, lives there too, waiting for his moment. Tonight, someone else strikes first.
screen: `A HOUSE MADE TO BURN.` → `A TUNNEL UNDER THE FLOOR.` → `TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kunti gives a feast. Brahmins come and eat, and women come, and when it's over the guests go home. But a Nishada woman, of the forest people, has come looking for food with her five sons. They eat and drink, and fall asleep in the house so heavily, the text says, they're like the dead. In the dark, Bhima gets up. He sets fire first to where Purochana sleeps, then to the door, then all around the house. The family goes down into the tunnel, and out. In the morning the townspeople stand at the ashes, grieving. They find Purochana, burned in his own trap. And they find a woman and five young men, and they say: Kunti and her sons are dead. The text never names them, and doesn't stop to judge the act. But the same epic gives us a way to see them. Later in the Mahabharata, in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the wise look with an equal eye on a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcast. It's called sama-darshana, the equal eye. Behind it sits one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the same atman, the Self, lives in every being. Nobody is background. A forest woman the town mistook for a queen, whom the poem never named, carries the same Self as Kunti. The lac house was built to kill the Pandavas. It killed the man who built it, and six people nobody planned for.

segments.voice: This one has a cost, so go slowly. If you have water near you, pour a little into a cup. In Pitru Paksha, many Hindus offer water, tarpana, for the dead, and some of those prayers include people with no family left to remember them. Bring to mind someone caught up in something that wasn't theirs: a stranger in the news, someone whose name you never learned. Hold them in attention, the way the story doesn't stop to. If you pray, offer the water for them. If you don't, simply hold them, and know they count.

738.title: Vidura's boat at the Ganga
738.hook: Bhima carries his family through the dark, and a boat carries them over the Ganga: why Hindus call holy places fords
738.carry: a tirtha is a crossing to the far shore
738.tomorrow: what does Bhima do with his anger?
738.howItsDone: Hindus go on tirtha yatra, pilgrimage, to holy fords and riverbanks such as Haridwar and Varanasi on the Ganga, to bathe, pray and remember their dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house burned, and strangers' bodies were taken for the Pandavas'. Your line: the wise see one self in every being.

Out of the tunnel, into a forest at night, with a town about to wake behind them. Kunti and her sons are worn out, and the dark is thick. So Bhima picks them all up. The text sets it out: his mother on his shoulders, the twins against his sides, Yudhishthira and Arjuna held by the hand. He pushes through the trees, carrying his whole family at once. The house is behind them. They still have to get away.
screen: `OUT OF THE TUNNEL.` → `BHIMA CARRIES THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: They reach the Ganga, and a man is waiting with a boat. He says Vidura sent him. But anyone could say that. So he gives a sign: he speaks back words from Vidura's warning on the road, words only Yudhishthira understood. Yudhishthira hears them, and the family gets in. Now look at where it ends: a crossing. The family goes over the Ganga, from the shore where, in everyone's eyes, they died, to a far bank where no one is looking for them. Hindus have a word for a place like that: tirtha. It literally means a ford, a crossing place in a river. It's also the word for a holy place of pilgrimage. Haridwar and Varanasi, on the Ganga, are great tirthas, and pilgrims travel there to bathe and pray. Underneath is an old Hindu picture: life itself is a river to cross. Samsara, the round of birth and death, is the near shore, and freedom is the far one. A hymn many Hindus sing, Bhaja Govindam, calls samsara the sea so hard to cross, and asks Krishna to keep us safe in it by his grace. A tirtha is where the far shore feels close. So the boatman carries them over, sends them on with good wishes, and goes back the way he came. And the Pandavas, dead as far as the world knows, step off on the far bank as people no one is looking for.
screen: `A BOAT, AND VIDURA'S WORDS.` · `TIRTHA: A FORD, A CROSSING.` · `SAMSARA: A RIVER TO CROSS.` · then, large: `CARRIED TO THE FAR SHORE.`

segments.voice: Let the chair or the floor take your whole weight, the way Kunti let Bhima carry her through the dark. If you have water near you, touch a drop to your head, the way pilgrims do at a tirtha. Bring to mind something you're crossing right now, a move, an ending, a change, and the far bank you hope for. If you pray, ask, as the old hymn does, for grace on the crossing. If you don't, just picture the far shore, and breathe as if you're already halfway over.
Nauka, the boat waiting at the Ganga, its boatman proved trustworthy by repeating Vidura's own hidden words.

739.title: Bhima keeps watch
739.hook: the city mourns the living, and in the forest Bhima holds his anger and keeps watch
739.carry: krodha, anger, is an enemy within
739.tomorrow: who rises out of a king's fire?
739.howItsDone: Offering water for the dead, called tarpana, is part of Hindu funeral and remembrance rites; in this story the offering is made for the Pandavas while they are still alive.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the boat at the Ganga, carrying the family to the far bank. Your line: a tirtha is a crossing to the far shore.

In Hastinapura, the news arrives: the Pandavas are dead, burned at Varanavata with their mother. Dhritarashtra weeps, the text says, and orders the rites for the dead. Water is offered for them. The people mourn. Vidura grieves only a little, because he knows. Far away, the five brothers and their mother are alive, asleep on the ground. Two places, and two kinds of grief.

In the forest they've gone as far as they can. Kunti is exhausted and thirsty. Bhima goes for water, and by the time he's back they're all asleep on the bare ground under a tree. So Bhima sits up alone and looks at them. The text gives him a lament here. In paraphrase: what could hurt more than this, my brothers sleeping on the earth, my mother lying in the open. He thinks of Duryodhana, and his anger rises. He could go back and end it, he says. But Yudhishthira isn't angry, and Bhima won't move without him. So he stays, and keeps watch. Hinduism has a name for what Bhima is holding: krodha, anger. Many Hindu teachers count it among the six inner enemies, with desire, greed, delusion, pride and envy. And in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna traces how it ruins a person: from craving comes anger, from anger confusion, from confusion you forget what matters, and then your judgment goes, and you fall. Notice the teaching isn't that Bhima shouldn't feel it. His anger is about something real. The teaching is that it mustn't drive. The brother known for his strength doesn't crush his anger, and doesn't obey it. He sits with it, and turns its heat into keeping watch, so the others can rest. In the city, a king weeps for nephews his own son tried to kill. In the forest, the brother known for his temper spends it sitting still.
screen: `ASLEEP ON THE BARE GROUND.` · `BHIMA'S LAMENT, AND HIS ANGER.` · `KRODHA: AN INNER ENEMY.` · then, large: `ANGER FELT, NOT OBEYED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that makes you angry right now, something real. Notice where it sits: jaw, chest, hands. Don't push it away, and don't feed it. Breathe out slowly. If you pray, say what many Hindus say at the end of a prayer: Om shanti, shanti, shanti, peace three times. If you don't, just breathe the heat down a little. Then picture someone asleep you'd watch over, and let that be where the strength goes.
Bhima, the brother known for strength and anger, who spends this night sitting still, keeping watch while his family sleeps.
Your line: krodha, anger, is an enemy within. Bhima felt it, and kept watch instead. Day seven hundred thirty-nine, done.

740.title: The daughter of the fire
740.hook: a king's fire offering gives him a son and a daughter: why Hindus still make offerings into fire
740.carry: yajna, offer to the fire, and blessing returns
740.howItsDone: Draupadi is honored as a goddess in parts of South India: some villages in Tamil Nadu keep temples to Draupadi Amman and hold festivals in her name, some with firewalking.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bhima under the tree, awake while his family slept. Your line: krodha, anger, is an enemy within.

A king has a fire lit because he wants a son. Drupada of Panchala has been humbled by Drona, and he wants someone who can answer that. Priests perform a great sacrifice. From the fire a young man rises, armed and shining: Dhrishtadyumna. Then, from the middle of the altar, a young woman. Dark, the text says, with eyes like lotus petals, and the scent of blue lotus around her. The sacrifice was for a son. The fire gives a daughter too.
screen: `A FIRE FOR A SON.` → `A DAUGHTER FROM THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: As she rises, the text says, a voice is heard from the sky: this dark girl will bring about the destruction of the warrior class. She's named Krishnaa, the dark one, and Draupadi, Drupada's daughter, and Panchali, the princess of Panchala. Hindus also call her Yajnaseni: the one born from the sacrifice. That sacrifice is a yajna, one of Hinduism's oldest practices. Offerings of ghee and grain are poured into a sacred fire, and Agni, the fire god, carries them up to the gods. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna puts the idea simply: nourish the gods with your offering, and the gods will nourish you; caring for each other, both reach the highest good. Drupada's yajna is that exchange made dramatic. He offers into the fire, and the fire gives back two children. Hindus still do this on a smaller scale. A havan, a home fire offering, is lit for a new house, a wedding, a fresh start, with the family tossing in ghee and grain while the priest says svaha. The same old shape: something given away in fire, and blessing hoped for in return. Back in the story, the Pandavas, still hiding as brahmins in a town, hear it all from a traveling brahmin: the fire, the brother and sister, and the swayamvara Drupada has announced, a princess's own choosing of a husband among gathered suitors. Kunti sees her sons grow restless, the text says, and says it's time to go to Panchala. So they set out, still dressed as brahmins.

The arena at Panchala is packed. Kings and princes have come from far and wide, dressed in their best. Brahmins have come to watch. There's music, and the noise of a crowd that has waited for this. Somewhere among the brahmins sit five brothers in borrowed clothes, whom everyone here believes are dead. Then Draupadi enters, carrying a garland, and her brother Dhrishtadyumna rises to announce the terms.

segments.voice: Here's the challenge, in paraphrase. This is the bow, these are the arrows. Up high is a mark, and in front of it a device set in the air, with an opening in it. Whoever strings the bow, shoots through the opening and hits the mark, and is worthy in birth and form and strength, wins my sister. Now a detail the text gives. Drupada had hoped all along to give his daughter to Arjuna, so he had this bow made so stiff that hardly anyone could string it. One by one, the kings try, and the bow beats them. Some can't bend it at all. Some get close, and it springs back and throws them to the ground, their crowns and ornaments scattered across the floor. Great names, humbled in front of everyone. Hindu teachers have a word for what hits the floor with those crowns: ahamkara, the ego, literally the I-maker. It's the part of us that says: I'm the one doing this, I deserve this, everyone is watching me. In the Gita, Krishna says the self confused by ahamkara thinks, I am the doer, when it's nature's forces doing the work. Hinduism doesn't ask you to stop acting. It asks you to act without that swelling I. Many tellers read the swayamvara this way: kings who walked up sure of their own names, thrown down by a bow that didn't care who they were. Tomorrow, someone very different walks up to the bow.

As the kings give up, one by one, a man rises whom we've met before. Karna. Found in a basket on the river, raised by a charioteer, born with armor on his body. The bow has just thrown kings to the floor in front of everyone. Karna walks up to it.

segments.voice: In the version Ganguli translated, Karna lifts the bow and strings it. He fits the arrows. He's about to shoot. And Draupadi speaks, loudly, so the whole arena hears. In paraphrase: I will not choose a suta for my husband. A suta: a charioteer, a charioteer's son. Karna laughs, a bitter laugh, the text says. He glances up at the sun, and puts the bow down. Readers hear Draupadi's line in different ways: holding the contest to the terms her brother read out, which counted birth; guarding her father's hope for Arjuna; or the old sting of birth used against a man who could clearly do the thing. The poem doesn't settle it. But stay with the glance. The sun, as we know and the arena doesn't, is Karna's father: Surya, the sun god. And for Hindus the sun isn't only a star. In the Rig Veda, Surya is the eye of the gods, the one who sees everything. Hindus still greet him every morning: pouring water toward the rising sun, an offering called arghya, or bowing to him in Surya namaskar. Later in this poem, Karna himself is a devoted worshipper of the sun. So here's what this moment holds. The arena looks at Karna and sees a charioteer's son. Surya, who sees everything, sees his own son. And Karna looks up to him at the moment he's turned away, without knowing whose face he's looking for. Karna and Draupadi will meet again in another hall, later in this serial. For now the bow is back on the ground, and the arena waits for someone else.

It shines on you no matter what anyone calls you.
